title: Cinderella (Aschenputtel)
full_text:
The wife of a rich man fell mortally ill. Calling her only daughter to her bedside, she whispered: "Dear child, remain pious and good, and heaven will always protect you; I shall look down upon you from above." Then she closed her eyes in peace.

When winter came, snow covered the mother's grave like a white cloth. When the spring sun melted it, the man took another wife. The stepmother brought two daughters into the house, who were fair of face but vile and black of heart.

They took away the girl's fine clothes, dressed her in an old gray smock, gave her wooden clogs, and forced her into the kitchen. From dawn till dusk, she carried heavy water buckets, lit fires, cooked, and washed. In the evening, having no bed, she had to lie in the hearth ashes, so that she was always dusty and dirty; and therefore they called her Aschenputtel (Cinderella).

When the father went to the fair, he asked the two stepdaughters what gifts he should bring them. The eldest demanded pearls and diamonds; the second wanted fine silks. But Cinderella said: "Father, break off the first twig that strikes against your hat on your way home, and bring it to me."

The father brought her a hazel twig. Cinderella carried it to her mother's grave, planted it in the soil, and wept over it so bitterly that her tears watered the twig. It grew into a magnificent hazel tree. Three times a day, Cinderella went to sit beneath it, weeping and praying; and each time, a gentle white bird flew into the branches, granting whatever wish she whispered from her heart.

The king proclaimed a grand three-day festival, inviting all the maidens in the realm so the prince might choose a bride. The two stepsisters dressed in embroidered velvet, while the cruel stepmother threw a dish of lentils into the hearth ashes, saying: "If you pick these clean in two hours, you may go!"

Cinderella went to the garden door and called:
"You tame pigeons, you turtledoves, and all you birds under heaven,
The good into the pot, the bad into the crop!"

Flocks of white doves swooped down, picking out every good lentil within an hour. But the stepmother laughed mockingly: "You have no dress, you cannot dance, and you would only bring shame upon us!" And she departed with her daughters.

Cinderella ran to her mother's grave beneath the hazel tree and called:
"Shiver and shake, dear little tree,
Throw gold and silver down upon me!"

The white bird threw down a dazzling robe of pure spun gold and silver, and slippers of silk and silver! Cinderella entered the palace, and the prince took her by the hand, dancing with no other maiden all evening. At nightfall, she slipped away like a deer and returned to her ashes.

On the third evening, the bird gave her a dress radiant as the sun, with slippers of solid gold. When she fled the ballroom at midnight, the prince, having coated the palace steps with pitch, found her left golden slipper stuck fast upon the stair!

The prince rode throughout the kingdom: "She alone shall be my bride whose foot fits this golden slipper!" The elder stepsister cut off her toe to force her foot into the slipper, but two white pigeons perched on the hazel tree sang:
"Rook di goo, rook di goo!
There's blood in the shoe!
The shoe is too small,
The true bride is left at the hall!"

The second sister cut off her heel, but the doves sang again of the blood in the shoe.

Then the prince asked: "Have you no other daughter?" The father replied: "Only a stunted kitchen drudge from my first wife."

When Cinderella washed the soot from her hands and face and stepped into the room, the golden slipper slid onto her delicate foot as if molded for it! The prince looked into her eyes and recognized the beautiful maiden who had danced with his heart.

They were wed with grand rejoicings, and the faithful white doves flew down to rest upon Cinderella's shoulders, accompanying the gentle queen through a long life of wisdom and peace.
moral: True goodness and modesty shine through the darkest ashes; patience is crowned with honor.

title: Snow White (Schneewittchen)
full_text:
Once upon a time in midwinter, when snowflakes fell like feathers from heaven, a queen sat sewing at a window with a black ebony frame. Pricking her finger with the needle, three drops of blood fell into the snow. The red looked so lovely upon the white that she thought: "Oh, that I had a child as white as snow, as red as blood, and as black as the wood of this ebony frame!"

Soon after, she bore a little daughter who was as white as snow, as red as blood, and with hair as black as ebony; and she was named Snow White. But when the child was born, the good queen died.

A year later, the king married a proud, vain queen who possessed a magical mirror. Every morning she stepped before it and asked:
"Mirror, mirror, on the wall,
Who in this realm is the fairest of all?"
And the mirror answered:
"You, my queen, are the fairest of all."

When Snow White grew to be seven years old, her beauty blossomed like the dawn. The queen asked her mirror, and it replied:
"Queen, you are full fair, 'tis true,
But Snow White is a thousand times fairer than you!"

Envy turned the queen's heart green and yellow. She ordered a huntsman to take Snow White into the deep forest and slay her. But seeing the child's innocent tears, the huntsman took pity on her: "Run away, poor child!" and brought back the lungs and liver of a wild boar to deceive the queen.

Snow White ran over sharp stones and through briars until she found a charming little cottage nestled among the trees. Inside, seven little beds were neatly made, and seven little plates stood upon the table. Famished and weary, she ate a little from each plate, drank a drop from each cup, and fell asleep in the seventh bed.

The cottage belonged to seven dwarfs who mined for gold and copper in the mountains. Returning with lanterns, they found the sleeping maiden: "Heavens! What a lovely child!" When she awoke and told her tale, they said: "Keep our house, cook, knit, and spin, and you shall dwell with us in peace!"

Three times the wicked queen learned from her mirror that Snow White was alive, and three times she came disguised over the mountains to destroy her: first with a suffocating lace bodice, then with a poisoned comb, and finally with an apple—its white side sweet, but its red cheek laden with mortal poison. When the queen bit the white side to prove it safe, Snow White took a bite of the red, and fell dead upon the floor!

The weeping dwarfs could not bury her in the black earth. They crafted a transparent coffin of pure crystal glass, wrote her royal name in letters of gold, and set it upon the mountain peak, with owls, ravens, and doves keeping vigil.

Years passed, yet Snow White lay uncorrupted, fresh as if asleep. A king's son came to the mountain, fell in love with the silent maiden, and begged the dwarfs for the coffin. As the prince's servants carried it down the crags, one stumbled over a tree root. The sudden jolt dislodged the piece of poisoned apple from Snow White's throat!

She opened her eyes, lifted the glass lid, and smiled: "Where am I?"

"You are with me!" rejoiced the prince.

Their royal wedding was celebrated with great splendor. The wicked queen, summoned to the feast, choked on her own venomous rage when she beheld the living bride, and fled into the dark wilderness, never to be heard from again; while Snow White and her prince ruled their kingdom in harmony and love.
moral: Envy consumes its own host; purity of soul overcomes the snares of malice.

title: Sleeping Beauty (Dornröschen)
full_text:
Long ago, a king and queen longed for a child. One day while the queen was bathing, a frog hopped out of the water and prophesied: "Before a year passes, you shall bring a daughter into the world!"

The prophecy came true, and the king was so overjoyed that he held a magnificent christening banquet. He invited not only his relatives, but the wise fairy women of the realm. There were thirteen in his kingdom, but having only twelve golden plates, one had to remain uninvited.

At the feast, the fairies bestowed miraculous gifts upon the infant princess: virtue, beauty, riches, and wisdom. Eleven had spoken when the uninvited thirteenth fairy burst into the hall, eyes flashing with vengeful spite. She cried in a loud voice: "In her fifteenth year, the king's daughter shall prick her finger on a spinning spindle and drop down dead!"

A shudder ran through the assembly. Then the twelfth fairy stepped forward; she could not undo the dark curse, but she could soften it: "It shall not be death, but a deep sleep of one hundred years into which the princess shall fall!"

The king, hoping to save his child, issued a royal decree banning every spinning wheel and spindle throughout the kingdom, ordering them burned to ashes.

The maiden grew into radiant youth, beloved for her gentle grace. On the day she turned fifteen, while exploring the old castle towers, she climbed a narrow winding stair to a forgotten garret. In the room sat an ancient woman spinning flax.

"What is that merry thing that rattles and hums?" asked the curious princess, reaching out her hand. The moment she touched the spindle, the ancient prophecy was fulfilled: the needle pricked her finger, and she sank down upon the bed in a profound slumber.

The deep sleep fell upon the entire palace! The king and queen fell asleep on their thrones; the courtiers fell asleep in the council chamber; the horses fell asleep in the stables, the hounds in the courtyard, the pigeons upon the roof, and the flies upon the wall! Even the hearth fire ceased its crackling, the roasting spit stopped turning, and the wind died down so that not a leaf stirred on the trees.

Around the castle grew a dense hedge of wild thorn briars. Year by year it grew taller, until it covered the battlements, towers, and flags, so that nothing of the castle could be seen. Across the land spread the legend of Dornröschen (Briar Rose), and many brave princes attempted to force their way through the hedge, but the thorns seized them like iron claws, and they perished miserably.

When the hundred years had passed, a young prince arrived in the province. An old peasant told him of the enchanted castle and the sleeping maiden. The prince boldly approached the thorn hedge; but lo! The hundred years were complete! The thorns transformed into a wall of blooming, fragrant roses that opened willingly to let him pass.

He walked through the silent halls where guards slept standing up with halberds in hand. At last he climbed the tower stairs and opened the garret door. There lay Briar Rose, looking so radiant and beautiful that he could not turn his eyes away. He bent down and kissed her lips.

At the touch of the kiss, Briar Rose opened her large, clear eyes and smiled at him.

The spell was broken! The princess arose, and with her awakened the king, the queen, the horses, the hounds, and the pigeons. The fire leaped up on the hearth, the meat began to roast again, and the royal wedding was celebrated with music and joy, living happily to the end of their days.
moral: Even when malice casts a dark shadow, destiny preserves goodness until the appointed hour of dawn.

title: Little Red Riding Hood (Rotkäppchen)
full_text:
Once upon a time, there was a sweet little village girl who was loved by everyone who looked at her, but most of all by her grandmother, who gave her a little cape of red velvet. It suited her so well that she would wear nothing else, and so she was called Little Red Riding Hood (Rotkäppchen).

One morning, her mother said: "Here, Little Red Riding Hood, take this cake and bottle of wine to your grandmother; she is weak and ill, and they will do her good. Walk nicely and quietly along the path, and do not stray into the forest, or you might fall and break the bottle!"

"I will take great care," promised the little girl.

The grandmother lived half an hour's walk away in the deep oak forest. When Red Riding Hood entered the woods, a wolf met her. The child did not know what a wicked beast he was, and was not afraid of him.

"Good day, Little Red Riding Hood!" said the wolf softly.
"Good day, wolf!"
"Where are you going so early?"
"To grandmother's, to take her fresh cake and wine."
"Where does grandmother live?"
"Under the three large oak trees near the hazel hedge," said the innocent child.

The wolf thought: "What a tender, juicy morsel! She will taste even sweeter than the old woman!" He pointed to the sunny glade: "Look at the lovely bluebells and yellow buttercups! Why don't you gather a fresh bouquet for your grandmother?"

Red Riding Hood thought: "A fresh bouquet will bring grandmother joy!" She left the path and wandered among the flowers, running from one bloom to the next.

Meanwhile, the wolf ran straight to the grandmother's cottage, knocked on the door, and spoke in a disguised voice: "It is Little Red Riding Hood with cake and wine!"

"Press the latch, my dear!" called the grandmother from her bed.

The wolf leaped in, swallowed the poor old grandmother whole, put on her nightgown and frilly nightcap, drew the bed-curtains, and lay down in the bed.

When Red Riding Hood had gathered as many flowers as she could carry, she ran to the cottage. Finding the door open, she felt an eerie dread. She entered the bedroom:
"Good morning, grandmother!" but received no answer. She drew the curtains.

"Oh, grandmother, what big ears you have!"
"The better to hear you with, my child!"
"Oh, grandmother, what big eyes you have!"
"The better to see you with!"
"Oh, grandmother, what big hands you have!"
"The better to hug you with!"
"Oh, but grandmother, what a terrible big mouth you have!"
"The better to eat you with!"

The wolf leaped from the bed and swallowed poor Little Red Riding Hood whole! Having satisfied his appetite, the beast lay down again and fell into a loud, snoring sleep.

A brave huntsman passed the house, thinking: "How loudly the old woman snores! I must see if she needs aid."

Peering through the window, he saw the wolf lying in the bed! "Have I found you at last, old sinner?" said the huntsman. He raised his rifle, but thought: "Perhaps the beast has swallowed the grandmother whole, and she may yet be saved!"

He took a pair of heavy shears and carefully snipped open the sleeping wolf's belly. After a few cuts, a little red cape gleamed forth! Out stepped Little Red Riding Hood, crying: "Oh, how dark and terrifying it was inside the wolf!" Then the old grandmother came out alive, though scarcely able to breathe.

Red Riding Hood gathered heavy field stones, with which they filled the wolf's belly, sewing it up neatly. When the wolf woke and tried to leap up to flee, the heavy stones dragged him down, and he collapsed dead upon the floor.

The huntsman took the wolf's pelt, the grandmother ate the cake and drank the wine, and Little Red Riding Hood thought: "Never again in my life will I stray from the path when my mother has forbidden it!"
moral: Disobeying wise counsel and straying from the honest path invites dangerous predators.

title: Hansel and Gretel (Hänsel und Gretel)
full_text:
Beside a great forest lived a poor woodcutter with his wife and his two children: the boy was named Hansel and the girl Gretel. They had little to bite and sup, and when a severe famine struck the land, he could no longer procure daily bread.

At night, the selfish stepmother persuaded the weak father: "Tomorrow at dawn we will lead the children into the thickest part of the forest, give them a crust of bread, and leave them; we cannot feed four mouths!" The father grieved, but surrendered to her insistence.

The children, awake from hunger, heard everything. Gretel wept, but Hansel whispered: "Be quiet, Gretel, do not sorrow; I will find a way!"

Hansel crept outside in the moonlight, filled his pockets with white pebbles that shone like silver coins, and returned to bed.

At dawn, as they were led into the deep woods, Hansel lagged behind, dropping a white pebble on the path every ten paces. When evening fell and the parents abandoned them by a fire, the children waited until the full moon rose. The white pebbles glittered like silver, guiding them straight back to their father's door! The father rejoiced, for it had broken his heart to leave them.

Soon, famine struck again, and the stepmother locked the door so Hansel could not gather pebbles. This time, Hansel crumbled his single crust of bread in his pocket, dropping crumbs along the path. But when the moon rose, the bread was gone: thousands of forest birds had eaten every crumb!

Lost in the vast wilderness, the children wandered for three days until they saw a charming snow-white bird singing upon a bough. They followed it to a strange little clearing.

Lo! There stood a miraculous cottage! The roof was made of gingerbread, the walls of rich cake, and the clear windowpanes of sparkling sugar candy!

Famished, Hansel broke off a piece of the roof, and Gretel nibbled on a round windowpane. A sweet, raspy voice called from within:
"Nibble, nibble, little mouse,
Who is nibbling at my house?"

The children answered: "The wind, the wind, the heavenly child!"

The door flew open, and out hobbled an ancient woman leaning on a crutch. She smiled with sweet words, invited them inside, and fed them milk, pancakes, apples, and nuts, putting them to sleep in clean white beds.

But the old woman was a wicked cannibal witch who built gingerbread houses to lure children!

At dawn, she seized Hansel and locked him in a grated iron stall, fattening him up for her cauldron, while forcing poor Gretel to cook and scrub. Every morning the half-blind witch cried: "Hansel, stretch out your finger that I may feel if you are fat enough!" But clever Hansel held out a dry chicken bone; and the blind witch, feeling the thin bone, wondered why he remained lean.

After four weeks, impatient to feast, the witch ordered Gretel: "Crawl into the oven and see if it is hot enough to bake!" intending to shut the iron door and roast Gretel alive.

Gretel saw the trap and said innocently: "I do not know how; the opening is too small!"

"Stupid goose!" rasped the witch. "The door is big enough; look, even I could get in!" She leaned her head into the oven.

Gretel gave a mighty push! She shoved the wicked witch right inside, slammed the iron door, and bolted it fast!

Gretel unlocked Hansel's stall: "Hansel, we are saved! The old witch is gone!"

In the witch's house, they found chests filled with pearls and precious gems. Filling their pockets, they reached a great lake where a kind white duck carried them across one by one.

They ran across the fields and burst into their father's cottage, throwing their arms around his neck! The cruel stepmother had died in their absence; and Hansel and Gretel emptied their pockets of shining jewels, living with their loving father in perpetual abundance, joy, and peace.
moral: Mutual love, presence of mind, and courage overcome the darkest perils of life.

title: Rapunzel
full_text:
A husband and wife lived beside a witch's walled garden where lush green rampion (rapunzel) salad grew. The pregnant wife longed so desperately for the rampion that she fell ill. The husband climbed the wall at twilight to steal a handful, but on the second night, the powerful enchantress, Dame Gothel, caught him: "How dare you steal my rampion? You shall pay for this!"

The terrified man begged for mercy, and the witch decreed: "You may take all the rampion you desire; but when the child is born, you must surrender it to me; I will raise it like a mother."

When the child was born, Dame Gothel appeared, named the lovely girl Rapunzel, and took her away.

Rapunzel grew into the most beautiful maiden in the world. When she turned twelve, the enchantress shut her in a high stone tower in the deep forest, having neither stairs nor door, but only a tiny window at the very top.

When the enchantress wished to enter, she stood below and called:
"Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
Let down your hair to me!"

Rapunzel had magnificent, long, golden hair that shone like spun gold. She fastened her tresses around a window hook, let them tumble twenty yards to the ground, and the witch climbed up them into the tower.

Years passed. A king's son rode through the forest and heard a singing voice so exquisite that he stood spellbound. It was Rapunzel, easing her solitude with sweet melodies. The prince watched and saw how the witch gained entrance.

The next evening, the prince went to the tower and called:
"Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
Let down your hair to me!"

The golden tresses fell, the prince climbed up, and Rapunzel was startled; but the prince spoke with such tender reverence and pure love that she placed her hand in his: "I will go with you, my prince; bring a skein of silk each time you visit, and I will weave a ladder to climb down."

Their secret happiness was betrayed when Rapunzel innocently asked Dame Gothel: "Tell me, godmother, why are you so much heavier to pull up than the young prince?"

Enraged, the enchantress shrieked: "Wicked child! You have deceived me!" In fury, she seized shears and hacked off Rapunzel's golden braids, banishing the poor maiden to a desolate wilderness.

That evening, the witch fastened the severed hair to the window hook. When the prince called, she let it down. When the prince climbed into the chamber, he met not his beloved, but the venomous gaze of the sorceress: "The bird is flown, and the cat will scratch out your eyes!"

In despair, the prince leaped from the high tower. He escaped with his life, but the sharp thorn briars beneath pierced his eyes, blinding him.

Blind and heartbroken, the prince wandered through the wilderness for years, eating roots and weeping for his lost bride. At last, he reached the desolate waste where Rapunzel lived with their twin children.

He heard a voice singing that resonated in his soul! He ran toward it; Rapunzel recognized him, threw her arms around his neck, and wept.

Two of her warm tears of love fell upon his blind eyes! Instantly, the clouds cleared, and his sight was completely restored, clearer and brighter than before!

The prince led Rapunzel and their children home to his kingdom, where they were received with boundless joy and reigned in peace, righteousness, and eternal love.
moral: True devotion endures suffering and blindness, guided by love toward healing and joy.

title: Rumpelstiltskin (Rumpelstilzchen)
full_text:
A boastful miller told the king: "I have a daughter who can spin straw into pure gold!"

The greedy king commanded the maiden to court, locked her in a chamber filled with straw, and ordered: "Spin this straw into gold before dawn, or you shall die!"

The poor miller's daughter wept in despair. Suddenly, a tiny little manikin stepped through the door: "What will you give me if I spin it for you?"

She gave him her necklace, and the imp sat at the wheel: whir, whir, whir! By sunrise, the room was filled with golden bobbins.

The king was thrilled, but his greed was boundless. The next night, he locked her in a larger room; she gave the little man her ring, and again the straw became gold.

On the third night, in an enormous hall of straw, the maiden had nothing left to give. The little man demanded: "Promise me your first-born child when you become queen!" Having no other choice to save her life, she promised.

The king married the miller's daughter. A year later, the young queen gave birth to a beautiful infant, having forgotten the imp.

Suddenly, the little man stepped into her bedchamber: "Now give me what you promised!"

The queen wept, offering all the treasures of the realm to keep her child. Moved by her tears, the manikin said: "I will give you three days; if you can discover my true name, you may keep your child!"

The queen sent messengers across the world to collect every name under heaven. On the first night, she guessed: "Caspar, Melchior, Balthazar!" On the second night: "Ribs-of-Beef, Sheepshanks, Spindleshanks!" But to each, the imp laughed: "That is not my name!"

On the third evening, a messenger returned from the deep forest: "High on a mountain where the fox and hare bid goodnight, I saw a fire burning; and around the fire hopped a comical little man on one leg, singing:
'Today I brew, tomorrow I bake,
Next day the queen's fair child I take;
For little does anyone know my fame,
That Rumpelstiltskin is my name!'"

When the little man arrived at dawn, demanding: "What is my name, Queen?", she asked calmly:
"Is your name Conrad?" "No!"
"Is your name Harry?" "No!"
"Can your name perhaps be... Rumpelstiltskin?"

"The devil told you that! The devil told you that!" shrieked the little man in a fury. He stamped his right foot so deep into the earth that his leg sank in up to his waist; then in his rage, he seized his left foot with both hands and tore himself in two!

The queen embraced her child in peace, freed forever from the shadow of the greedy imp.
moral: Boasting traps us in impossible debts; steadfast maternal love unmasks deceit.

title: The Frog Prince (Froschkönig)
full_text:
In olden times, when wishing still helped, lived a king whose daughters were all handsome, but the youngest was so beautiful that the sun itself marvelled whenever it shone upon her.

Near the king's castle lay a dark forest, and in the forest beneath an ancient linden tree was a cool spring. On hot days, the young princess would sit by the well, tossing her favorite toy—a golden ball—high into the air and catching it.

One afternoon, the golden ball slipped through her fingers, bounced upon the ground, and plunged straight into the deep water of the well. The princess wept bitterly, for the spring was so deep that no bottom could be seen.

As she wept, an ugly frog poked its head from the water: "Why do you weep so bitterly, King's daughter?"

"My golden ball has fallen into the well!" she sobbed.

"I will fetch it for you," said the frog, "if you promise that I shall be your companion, sit beside you at your table, eat from your golden plate, drink from your cup, and sleep in your little bed."

The princess thought: "What nonsense the silly frog talks! He lives in the water with his fellows; he cannot be a companion to human beings!" So she promised everything, only wanting her ball back.

The frog dove into the depths and brought up the golden ball in its mouth, dropping it onto the grass. Overjoyed, the princess seized the ball and ran home, ignoring the frog's cries: "Wait for me! I cannot run as fast as you!"

The next day, as the royal family sat dining, a knock was heard at the door, and a voice called:
"Youngest king's daughter, open to me!
Remember the promise beneath the tree!"

The princess went to open the door, saw the slimy frog, and slammed the door shut in terror.

The wise old king saw her distress and asked what frightened her. When she confessed her promise at the well, the king spoke with firm royal majesty: "What you have promised, you must keep! Let the frog enter!"

The princess reluctantly obeyed. The frog hopped to her chair: "Lift me onto the table!" When lifted, he said: "Push your golden plate nearer, that we may eat together!" She did so with disgust, while the king watched with approval.

Finally, the frog said: "I am weary; carry me to your room that we may sleep in your silken bed."

The princess wept, horrified by the cold, clammy creature. But the king rebuked her: "You must not despise one who helped you when you were in distress!"

She carried the frog up to her chamber in two fingers, setting him in a corner. But when the frog hopped toward her bed, whispering: "Lift me up, or I will tell your father!", her patience snapped. She seized the frog and threw it against the wall with all her might: "Now you will have peace, you ugly frog!"

As he struck the wall, he tumbled down—not as a dead frog, but as a handsome young prince with noble, friendly eyes!

A wicked witch had enchanted him, and no one could release him but the king's daughter.

By her father's royal decree, they were betrothed. The next morning, a magnificent carriage drawn by eight white horses with golden plumes arrived, driven by Faithful Heinrich—the prince's devoted servant, who had bound three iron bands around his heart to keep it from breaking with grief during his master's enchantment.

As they rode to the prince's kingdom, three loud snaps were heard: the iron bands had burst from Faithful Heinrich's heart, overflowing with the joy of his master's freedom!
moral: What you have promised in your hour of need, you must faithfully fulfill in the hour of prosperity.

title: The Wolf and the Seven Young Kids
full_text:
An old mother goat had seven young kids whom she loved with all her heart. One day, preparing to go into the forest for food, she gathered them: "Dear children, I am going into the woods; beware of the wolf! If he enters, he will eat you all, skin and hair! He often disguises himself, but you will know him by his rough, gravelly voice and his pitch-black paws."

"We will take great care, mother," promised the kids.

Soon, a knock sounded at the door: "Open, dear children! Your mother is back with gifts for everyone!"

The kids heard the deep, raspy voice and called: "We will not open! You are not our mother; she has a soft, sweet voice, but your voice is rough: you are the wolf!"

The wolf went to a shopkeeper, bought a lump of chalk, and ate it to make his voice smooth and soft.

He returned and knocked: "Open, little ones, your mother has returned!"

He placed his paw on the window sill. The kids saw the black fur and cried: "We will not open! Our mother does not have black feet: you are the wolf!"

The wolf ran to a baker: "Rub some dough over my feet!" Then he ran to the miller: "Dust white flour over my paws!"

The wolf knocked a third time: "Open, children, your dear mother is here!" He showed his white paws at the window.

Deceived by the sweet voice and white feet, the kids unlatched the bolt. In sprang the wolf!

The terrified kids scrambled to hide: the first under the table, the second into the bed, the third into the stove, the fourth into the kitchen, the fifth into the cupboard, the sixth beneath the washing bowl, and the seventh into the tall clock-case!

The wolf found them and swallowed them whole, one after another—all except the youngest, who was hidden in the clock-case.

Satiated and heavy, the wolf lay down beneath a tree in the meadow and fell into a snoring sleep.

When the old mother goat returned and found her house ransacked, she wept bitter tears. The youngest kid leaped from the clock and told what had happened.

Weeping, the mother goat walked into the meadow and found the wolf snoring, with something kicking inside his bloated belly!

"Heavens!" she cried. "Can my poor children still be alive?"

She took shears and a needle. She cut open the beast's stomach, and out sprang the six little kids, alive and unhurt, for the greedy monster had swallowed them whole in his haste!

They gathered heavy field stones, filled the wolf's belly to the brim, and the mother sewed it up with deft stitches.

When the wolf woke, parched with thirst, he walked to the well to drink. The heavy stones threw him off balance; he tumbled into the deep well and drowned!

The seven kids and their mother danced around the well with joy, singing: "The wolf is dead! The wolf is dead!" and lived together in safety and peace.
moral: Heed the warnings of loving parents; smooth speech and white paws cannot conceal wolfish intentions.

title: The Bremen Town Musicians
full_text:
A donkey who had faithfully carried sacks to the mill for decades grew old and weak. Hearing his master plan to dispose of his hide, the donkey slipped away and set out on the road to Bremen: "I can become a town musician there!"

Along the way, he met a hunting hound panting by the ditch: "I am old and can no longer hunt, so my master wanted to shoot me!"

"Come with me to Bremen," invited the donkey. "I will play the lute, and you shall beat the kettledrums!"

A little further, they met a cat with a face like three rainy days: "My teeth are blunt, and I prefer sitting by the fire to hunting mice, so my mistress wanted to drown me!"

"Join us!" said the donkey. "You understand night-music; come to Bremen!"

Then they passed a farmyard where a rooster was crowing with all his might: "The cook is putting me into the Sunday soup tomorrow, so I crow while I still have a throat!"

"Come with us, Red-Comb!" said the donkey. "Anything is better than death; your voice will make splendid harmony!"

The four companions could not reach Bremen in one day. At nightfall in the deep forest, they spotted a light shining from a cottage window. The tall donkey looked inside: "I see a table spread with roasted meat, bread, and wine, and four fierce robbers feasting!"

Hungry and cold, the animals devised a plan.

The donkey placed his forefeet upon the window sill; the hound climbed upon the donkey's back; the cat scrambled upon the hound's shoulders; and the rooster flew up to perch upon the cat's head!

At a signal, they struck up their music together: the donkey brayed, the dog barked, the cat meowed, and the rooster crowed! Then they crashed through the windowpanes with a deafening clatter of shattering glass!

Terrified by the roaring monster, the robbers fled into the woods in utter panic.

The four musicians sat down at the table, ate the feast with boundless appetite, put out the light, and went to sleep: the donkey in the yard, the dog behind the door, the cat on the warm hearth ashes, and the rooster upon the roof beam.

At midnight, seeing the house quiet, the robber captain sent a henchman to scout the cottage.

The spy crept into the pitch-black kitchen. Seeing the glowing eyes of the cat, he mistook them for live coals and held a match to them. The furious cat spat and scratched his face with sharp claws!

Terrified, the robber ran for the back door, where the dog sprang up and bit his leg! In the yard, the donkey kicked him with full force; and from the roof, the rooster crowed triumphantly: "Cock-a-doodle-doo!"

The robber fled back to his captain, trembling: "In that house sits a hideous witch who scratched my face with long nails; behind the door stands a man with a knife who stabbed my leg; in the yard lies a black monster who struck me with a wooden club; and upon the roof sits the judge, shouting: 'Bring the rascal to me!' I barely escaped with my life!"

The robbers never dared return to the forest; and the four Bremen musicians found the cottage so cozy that they never left it, living together in friendship, music, and peace.
moral: Those discarded by the world can unite their humble strengths to win freedom and a peaceful home.

title: The Fisherman and His Wife
full_text:
There was once a fisherman and his wife who lived together in a filthy pigsty of a hovel close by the sea. Every day the fisherman went out with his rod and sat watching the clear water.

One afternoon, his line was pulled deep into the depths. He hauled up an enormous flounder, who spoke in human voice: "Fisherman, spare my life! I am no common fish, but an enchanted prince! Throw me back into the water, I pray you!"

The kind fisherman threw the flounder back: "I would not kill a fish that can speak!"

When he went home and told his wife Ilsebill, she flew into a rage: "Did you ask for nothing in return? It is dreadful to live in this dirty hovel! Go back and ask the fish for a snug little cottage!"

The fisherman went to the sea; the water was green and yellow. He called:
"Flounder, flounder in the sea,
Prithee, listen unto me:
For my wife, good Ilsebill,
Wills not as I'd have her will!"

The flounder popped up: "What does she want?"
"She wants a snug cottage."
"Go home; she has it already," said the fish.

The fisherman returned and found a lovely stone cottage with a parlor, garden, and chickens. He was happy, but after a week, Ilsebill grew discontented: "This cottage is too cramped! Go back and tell the flounder I must have a great stone castle with servants and horses!"

The fisherman's heart grew heavy, but he feared his wife. The sea was now dark blue and purple. The fish granted the castle.

Next, Ilsebill demanded to be king: "I must be King of the land!" The sea turned dark gray and foamy; the flounder made her king, with crowns and golden scepters.

Then she demanded: "I must be Emperor!" The sea turned black and stormy; the fish made her Emperor.

Then: "I must be Pope!" The sea heaved with violent breakers, and sky tore with wind; the fish made her Pope, crowned with triple tiaras.

Early the next morning, as the sun began to rise, Ilsebill looked upon the golden dawn from her bed, and shook with rage: "Why can I not command the sun and moon to rise? Go back to the fish! I must become like God Almighty!"

The fisherman trembled in sheer terror. Thunder crashed, lightning cleaved the sky, and mountainous black waves roared like doom. The fisherman shouted against the hurricane:
"Flounder, flounder in the sea,
Prithee, listen unto me:
For my wife, good Ilsebill,
Wills not as I'd have her will!"

The flounder surfaced in the storm: "What does she want now?"

"Alas!" wept the fisherman. "She wants to be like God!"

"Go home," spoke the flounder solemnly. "She sits already in her dirty pigsty."

And there they sit to this very day.
moral: Unbridled ambition and insatiable greed eventually strip away everything and return one to the hovel.

title: The Golden Bird
full_text:
A king possessed a pleasure garden containing a tree that bore golden apples. When the apples ripened, one was found missing each morning.

The king set his three sons to keep watch. The two elder princes fell asleep, but the youngest prince kept vigil and saw a bird whose feathers were of solid gold steal an apple. He shot an arrow, knocking loose a golden feather that shone brighter than all the lamps in the palace.

The king dispatched his sons to capture the miraculous bird.

On the road, the two elder brothers met a talking fox, who warned them: "Do not choose the luxurious, noisy inn, but stay at the humble roadside tavern!" The proud brothers mocked the fox, entered the grand inn, and squandered their money in foolish pleasures.

The youngest prince met the fox, thanked him for his advice, and stayed in the humble cottage.

The grateful fox said: "Sit upon my tail, and I will carry you!"

With lightning speed, the fox carried him to a castle where the golden bird sat in a wooden cage beside a golden cage. The fox warned: "Do not put the bird into the golden cage!" But the prince yielded to vanity, touched the golden cage, alarms rang, and he was captured.

The rival king demanded the Golden Horse that ran swifter than the wind as ransom. The fox helped him again, warning: "Do not use the golden saddle; use the leather saddle!" The prince forgot the warning, touched the gold saddle, and was caught again.

To redeem himself, he was sent to bring the Princess of the Golden Palace. The fox guided him, and the prince won the princess's heart through gentle courtesy.

With the fox's clever counsel, the prince outwitted both kings, carrying off the Golden Bird, the Golden Horse, and the beautiful Princess.

On the return journey, his two jealous brothers ambushed him, threw him into a deep gorge, and brought the treasures to their father, claiming they had won them. But the horse would not eat, the bird would not sing, and the maiden wept constantly.

The faithful fox descended into the gorge, rescued the youngest prince, and brought him disguised to the palace.

The moment the true prince entered the court, the bird sang with celestial joy, the golden horse began to feast, and the princess ran to embrace him with tears of happiness!

The treacherous brothers were exiled, and the youngest prince married the princess. Finally, at the fox's request, the prince touched the animal with his sword, breaking an ancient enchantment and restoring the fox to his true form as the princess's noble brother! And they reigned in peace and prosperity.
moral: Heeding the counsel of the wise and humble guides one past temptation to true victory.

title: The Twelve Brothers
full_text:
A king had twelve sons, and declared that if his thirteenth child was a daughter, all twelve princes must die so that her inheritance might be boundless.

The good queen warned her sons. Twelve white flags were hoisted on the tower as a signal that a sister was born; and the twelve brothers fled into the deep forest, taking shelter in an enchanted cottage.

When the princess turned ten, she discovered twelve shirts in her mother's chest, learned of her brothers' exile, and vowed to find them. Guided by love, she found their forest cottage and became their devoted little housekeeper.

One morning, wanting to please them, she plucked twelve white lilies blooming in the garden. Instantly, the twelve brothers were transformed into twelve black ravens, who flew away screaming over the treetops, and the cottage vanished!

An old fairy appeared: "You have bewitched your brothers! They can be restored only if you maintain absolute silence for seven years: you must not speak, laugh, or weep. If a single word escapes you, your brothers will die!"

The maiden climbed into a tall oak tree and sat spinning flax in total silence.

A hunting king discovered the beautiful mute maiden, fell in love with her innocence, and made her his queen.

The king's jealous mother accused the silent queen of sorcery and treason, whispering lies that led to her condemnation to the stake.

Even as the flames rose around the execution scaffold, the queen remained steadfastly silent, trusting heaven.

Just as the seventh year expired to the very second, a rushing sound filled the sky! Twelve black ravens swooped down from the clouds, their wings touching the earth.

Instantly, twelve magnificent princes stood before the throne! They extinguished the flames, embraced their devoted sister, and revealed her heroic sacrifice to the king, while the wicked mother-in-law was banished forever.
moral: Pure, patient silence in the face of false accusation possesses the power to redeem.

title: The Pack of Ragamuffins
full_text:
Chanticleer the rooster and Partlet the hen built a miniature carriage out of walnut shells, harnessed four mice to it, and drove toward the nut-hill.

On the road, they picked up a duck who had lost her web-shoes, a sewing needle who thought himself a knight, and a pin who carried a sharp point.

They arrived late at an inn, demanding shelter from a grumbling landlord. They promised the landlord the duck's eggs and the rooster's feathers.

Before dawn, after eating all the bread and cheese in the kitchen, the ragamuffins prepared their escape: the needle stuck himself into the landlord's shaving towel, the pin stuck into his chair cushion, and the eggshells buried themselves in the fireplace ashes.

When the landlord awoke, he blew upon the ashes, and the eggshells exploded into his eyes; he ran to wipe his face, and the needle scratched his nose; he sat down to rest, and the pin pricked his seat!

He ran to the door shouting for guards, while the rooster crowed from the road, driving the walnut carriage merrily into freedom!
moral: Unlikely rogues who band together can turn an unfair world upside down with laughter.

title: Brother and Sister
full_text:
Fleeing a cruel stepmother, a little brother and sister walked into the great forest. The wicked woman had bewitched all the forest brooks.

At the first brook, the water murmured: "Whoever drinks of me will become a tiger!" The sister caught her brother's arm: "Do not drink, or you will tear me to pieces!"

At the second brook, it sang: "Whoever drinks will become a wolf!" The sister held him back again.

At the third brook, parched with unbearable thirst, the boy could not resist and drank. Instantly, he was transformed into a gentle white fawn!

The sister wept, took off her golden garter, fastened it around the fawn's neck, and wove a rope of rushes to lead him to a deserted woodland hut, where they lived in sweet communion.

During a royal hunt, the king chased the beautiful fawn to the cottage. Enamored by the maiden's grace, the king brought them both to his castle and married the sister, while the fawn roamed freely through the royal gardens.

When the queen bore a son, the envious stepmother slipped into the palace, smothered the queen in a heated bath, and put her own ugly one-eyed daughter in the bed.

For three nights, the ghost of the queen appeared at midnight to nurse her baby and stroke the fawn's neck, whispering:
"How fares my child? How fares my fawn?
Twice come I here, then forever gone!"

On the third night, the king stayed awake, stepped forward, and embraced her: "You are my true, living wife!"

By God's grace, she returned to life! The wicked stepmother was condemned to justice, and as she perished, the enchantment broke: the white fawn stood up as a handsome youth, restored to his human form, living in lifelong joy with his sister.
moral: Patience and gentle affection outlast cruelty; innocence is vindicated by truth.

title: The Three Little Men in the Wood
full_text:
A cruel stepmother dressed her gentle stepdaughter in a thin paper dress and sent her into the snowy forest in midwinter to gather a basket of fresh ripe strawberries!

Shivering with cold, the maiden stumbled upon a tiny cottage where three little men (dwarfs) sat by the hearth. She greeted them with sweet courtesy, warmed herself modestly by the fire, and shared her single crust of dry bread with them.

Moved by her goodness, the three little men gave her a broom: "Sweep the snow from our back door!"

When she swept the snow, what did she find underneath? Sweet, ripe red strawberries growing in the snow!

As she departed, the three little men blessed her: the first made her grow more beautiful every day; the second decreed that a piece of gold should fall from her mouth whenever she spoke; and the third decreed that a king should marry her.

When the envious stepsister heard this, she wrapped herself in warm furs, took sweet cakes, and walked into the forest. Finding the cottage, she entered without greeting, sat on the best chair, ate her cakes without sharing, and refused to sweep the back door: "I am not your servant!"

The three dwarfs cursed her: she grew uglier each day; whenever she spoke, a toad hopped from her mouth; and she died in disgrace.

The gentle stepdaughter met a king, who marvelled at the gold coins that fell from her lips and made her his beloved queen, proving that genuine kindness receives heavenly reward.
moral: Kindness shown to strangers brings blessings upon one's lips; malice brings toads.

title: The Wishing-Table, the Gold-Ass, and the Cudgel in the Sack
full_text:
A tailor had three sons and a pet goat who lied to the father that the sons never fed her, driving the tailor to banish all three boys in anger.

The eldest son became a cabinet-maker and received a magical little table: whenever he said: "Table, be covered!", it set itself with roasted meats, wine, and pastries. On his way home, a greedy innkeeper switched the table for an ordinary one while he slept.

The second son became a miller and received a miraculous donkey: whenever he said: "Bricklebrit!", gold ducats fell from its mouth. The same dishonest innkeeper switched the donkey for a common beast.

The youngest son became a wood-turner. His master gave him a stout wooden cudgel inside a burlap sack: "Whenever someone tries to harm you, say: 'Cudgel, out of the sack!' and it will dance upon their backs until you bid it stop!"

The third son arrived at the same dishonest inn, boasting of his magical sack. At midnight, the thieving innkeeper crept into his room to steal it.

The youth shouted: "Cudgel, out of the sack!"

Out leaped the wooden cudgel! It rained heavy blows upon the innkeeper's shoulders, ribs, and legs until the thief shrieked for mercy, confessing his crimes and returning the magical wishing-table and the gold-ass!

The three brothers returned to their father's house, restored family peace, provided endless feasts with the table and gold with the donkey, and lived in lasting prosperity.
moral: Honest labor earns miraculous gifts; thieves who steal from the simple receive the cudgel of justice.

title: The White Snake
full_text:
A wise king was served every evening with a covered dish that none of his courtiers were permitted to see. The faithful servant, consumed by curiosity, lifted the lid one night and found a boiled white snake. He tasted a small morsel; and instantly, he understood the language of all animals!

That day, the queen lost her diamond ring. Suspected of theft, the servant went into the courtyard and overheard a duck complaining that an iron pebble had stuck in her throat. The servant had the cook examine the duck, found the ring, and cleared his name with honors.

Setting out to see the world, the servant helped three drowning fish in the shallows; spared an ant queen whose colony had been disturbed; and fed his horse to save three starving young ravens in an oak tree.

Arriving in a great kingdom, he competed for the hand of a princess. To win her, he had to perform three impossible tasks.

First, he was ordered to retrieve a golden ring thrown into the deep sea; the three grateful fish brought it up from the ocean bed!

Second, he was ordered to gather ten sacks of millet scattered across the grass in a single night; the grateful ant queen and her millions of ants gathered every single seed before dawn!

Third, he was ordered to bring the Golden Apple from the Tree of Life; the three ravens flew across the world to the garden of heaven and dropped the golden apple into his hands!

The princess recognized his nobility of soul and married him, living together in peace and mutual love.
moral: Kindness shown to the humblest creatures of earth returns as an invincible shield in times of trial.

title: The Straw, the Coal, and the Bean
full_text:
An old woman dropped a straw, a glowing coal, and a broad bean while preparing her hearth fire. The three companions escaped together, setting out to seek their fortune.

They reached a rushing brook with no bridge. The clever straw offered: "I will lay myself across the water; you two can walk over me like a bridge!"

The glowing coal stepped boldly onto the straw. But when it reached the middle, hearing the water roar beneath, it froze in terror. The burning coal scorched through the dry straw; snap! The straw broke in two, the coal fell into the water with a hiss, and both drowned!

The bean, who had stayed safely on the bank, laughed so uproariously at their clumsy mishap that she burst her own seams!

A wandering tailor took pity on the weeping bean, drew out needle and thread, and stitched her seam closed with black cotton. And that is why, to this very day, all broad beans have a black seam down their middle!
moral: Reckless laughter at another's misfortune often ends in bursting one's own seams.

title: The Fisherman and His Wife (The Lesson of the Sea)
full_text:
Once upon a time, upon the windswept shore of a gray northern sea, there lived a humble fisherman and his wife Ilsebill in a miserable little hovel fashioned from driftwood and sea grass. Every morning at dawn, the honest fisherman walked down to the water with his hemp line, wishing for nothing more than enough fish to provide a simple supper. One calm morning, a heavy pull tugged upon his hook, and he hauled ashore an enormous golden flounder. To his astonishment, the fish spoke with a pleading human voice: 'Spare my life, kind fisherman! I am no common creature of the deep, but an enchanted prince. Cast me back into the cool brine, and may good fortune follow you!' Moved with compassion, the honest man gently released the flounder back into the sea and returned home with empty hands and a peaceful heart.

When he arrived at his hut and recounted the day's wonder to his wife, Ilsebill’s face darkened with furious indignation. 'You foolish, simple-minded man!' she scolded, shaking her wooden ladle. 'To catch a magical talking prince and ask for nothing in return? Go back to the sea at once and demand a cozy stone cottage with a blooming herb garden, a tiled chimney, and a pantry full of smoked ham!' Reluctantly, the fisherman trudged back to the beach. The water was no longer clear green, but murky yellow and purple. He called upon the flounder, and the wish was granted without delay. Yet within a fortnight, the cozy cottage was too small for Ilsebill’s surging ambition. She ordered him back again and again—first for a majestic castle of carved marble, then to be crowned queen of the land, then emperor of the realm, and finally the supreme pope! With every new demand, the sea groaned and turned from dark violet to pitch black, boiling with angry white foam and crashing against the cliffs with terrifying thunder.

At last, waking before dawn in her papal bedchamber of crimson velvet, Ilsebill looked out at the morning sky and was seized by monstrous arrogance. Shaking her terrified husband awake, she shrieked: 'I cannot bear that the sun and moon should rise without my royal command! Go to the sea this instant and tell the flounder that I must become like God!' Trembling in dread, the weeping fisherman stumbled to the shore amid a howling hurricane that uprooted ancient oaks and split the blackened heavens with lightning. He screamed his wife’s terrible demand into the roaring surf. The magical flounder surfaced through the towering waves, looked upon the weeping man with mournful pity, and whispered softly: 'Go home, fisherman. She sits once more in her muddy hovel by the shore.' And there, amid the broken driftwood and sea grass, they remain to this day, a timeless warning that boundless greed destroys the very gifts it seeks to hoard.
moral: True abundance is found in gratitude for enough; boundless greed consumes itself.

title: The Brave Little Tailor
full_text:
A little tailor sat on his bench sewing when seven flies landed on his jam bread. Slapping with a cloth, he killed all seven at once!

"What a hero I am!" he cried. He embroidered a belt with gold letters: "Seven at One Blow!" and set out to conquer the world.

Meeting an enormous giant on the mountain, the tailor challenged him. When the giant crushed a rock in his fist, the tailor squeezed a lump of soft cheese until water dripped from his hand! When the giant threw a stone high into the clouds, the tailor tossed a live bird into the air that flew away over the peaks! The giant, thinking it was a stone that never returned, was terrified.

The king promised the tailor his daughter's hand and half his kingdom if he could vanquish two wild giants, a fierce unicorn, and a rampaging wild boar.

The brave little tailor tricked the two giants into fighting each other by dropping stones on their heads while they slept; he trapped the unicorn by making it drive its horn into an oak tree; and he lured the boar into an abandoned church and locked the door!

The astonished king had to keep his royal oath, and the little tailor married the princess and became a wise, victorious king, proving that intellect and audacity conquer every giant.
moral: Audacity, quick wit, and presence of mind conquer giants where brute force fails.

title: The Little Peasant
full_text:
In a small village nestled between rolling hills lived a clever peasant who was so poor that he owned not a single cow or goat, having only a tiny thatch cottage and an empty barn. When the wealthy village bailiff and rich farmers drove their plump cattle to pasture, they mocked the poor peasant: 'Look at the beggar who has no livestock!' Undaunted by their cruel taunts, the little peasant carved a realistic calf out of dry pine wood, painted it with black and white spots, and carried it out to the grassy pasture, instructing the village herdsman to let it graze in peace. When the herdsman returned at evening claiming the wooden calf had run away, the peasant brought him before the magistrate and was awarded an honest cow in compensation.

Envious of his good fortune, the greedy bailiff schemed to ruin him, forcing the peasant to slaughter the cow. Not one to despair, the peasant salted the meat and took the dried hide into town to sell. On his journey through a dark forest, night overtook him, and he took shelter in the loft of a lonely wayside inn. Peering down through a knothole in the floorboards, he watched the innkeeper’s wife entertaining an illicit feast of roast fowl and wine with a corrupt local cleric. When the master of the inn knocked on the door, the wife hurriedly hid the feast in the bake-oven and pushed the cleric inside a large wooden meal chest in the parlor!

The little peasant climbed down, knocked on the door, and offered his dry cow-skin to the innkeeper, claiming it was a magical fortune-teller. Squeezing the stiff leather under his arm so it squeaked, the peasant announced: 'My hide says there is a roasted goose and jug of wine hidden inside your bake-oven!' The astonished innkeeper opened the oven, found the feast, and shared it with the peasant. Squeezing the hide again, the peasant whispered: 'My hide says the devil himself is hiding in your meal chest!' The innkeeper unlocked the chest, and the soot-blackened cleric tumbled out in terror, running into the night while leaving behind a purse of three hundred gold thalers! The little peasant returned home wealthy and respected, proving that a sharp, resourceful mind can turn every obstacle into triumphant success.
moral: The simple man who relies on wits turns the greed of dishonest oppressors against themselves.

title: The Queen Bee
full_text:
Two elder princes went seeking adventure and fell into reckless, idle living. Their youngest brother, whom they called Simpleton (Dummling), went to bring them home.

Along the road, the elder brothers wanted to destroy an anthill, kill ducks on a pond, and smoke out a beehive. Dummling stood before them each time: "Leave them in peace; I will not suffer you to torment them!"

They arrived at an enchanted castle where all inhabitants were turned to stone. To break the spell, three tasks had to be solved:

First, collect a thousand pearls of the princess scattered under the moss in the forest; the grateful ants gathered every single pearl before sunset!

Second, fetch the key to the princess's bedchamber from the deep lake; the grateful ducks dove down and brought the key from the mud!

Third, identify the youngest and sweetest of the three sleeping princesses, whose lips looked identical; the grateful Queen Bee flew in and tasted the honey upon the lips of the true maiden!

The spell broke instantly: the castle awakened, and Dummling married the youngest princess, while his reformed brothers married her sisters, reigning in peace and gratitude.
moral: Kindness to the small and defenseless is rewarded with victory when the great tasks arrive.

title: The Three Feathers
full_text:
An old king blew three feathers into the air to determine which of his three sons should inherit the crown: the eldest followed the feather east; the second followed it west; and the third feather fell straight to the earth, where the youngest son, Simpleton, sat down in obedience.

Beside the fallen feather lay a trapdoor into the earth. Descending the stairs, the youth met an enormous fat toad surrounded by her little ones. The gentle toad rewarded his respectful courtesy with the finest carpet ever woven in the world.

His brothers brought coarse blankets, but Simpleton brought the miraculous carpet!

Next, the toad gave him a ring of dazzling gold and diamonds; and finally, the toad transformed into a breathtakingly beautiful maiden in a carriage made of a yellow carrot drawn by six white mice!

The court marveled at her grace, and the king placed the crown upon Simpleton's head, proving that humble trust in Providence outshines worldly ambition.
moral: The world mocks simplicity, but humble obedience to truth receives the kingdom.

title: The Golden Goose
full_text:
A young woodcutter called Dummling was despised by his family. When his elder brothers went to the forest, their mother gave them rich cakes and wine, but they refused to share with a little gray old man who asked for food, and were both injured by their axes.

When Dummling went to the woods with only cinder bread and sour beer, he gladly shared with the old man: "There is little, but what there is we will share together!"

The beer turned to sweet wine and the crust to rich cake. The old man said: "Because you have a good heart and share willingly, cut down that ancient oak and you will find a treasure at the roots."

At the root of the tree sat a goose whose feathers were of solid gold!

Dummling took the goose to an inn. At night, the innkeeper's eldest daughter tried to pluck a golden feather, and her hand was glued fast to the bird! The second daughter came to pull her away and was stuck to her sister! The third daughter touched her sister and was stuck fast too!

In the morning, Dummling tucked the goose under his arm and marched on, with the three sisters trailing behind! A parson shouted at them and was stuck; the sexton grabbed the parson and was stuck; two laborers tried to help and were glued fast—forming a comical procession of seven people hopping behind the golden goose!

They reached the royal capital, where the king's daughter suffered from deep melancholy and had never been known to laugh. The king had promised her hand to whoever could make her smile.

When the princess looked from her window and saw the solemn procession of seven people hopping in frantic helplessness behind Dummling and his golden goose, she burst into clear, ringing laughter!

Dummling married the princess and became a beloved king, proving that sharing with a generous heart brings joy and blessings to the whole world.
moral: A generous heart that shares simple bread unlocks laughter and brings joy to the kingdom.

title: All-Kinds-of-Fur (Allerleirauh)
full_text:
A king whose queen possessed golden hair was bound by a dying promise to marry only a maiden whose beauty matched hers. In his madness, he sought to marry his own gentle daughter.

To escape the unlawful union, the princess demanded three impossible gifts: a dress golden as the sun, a dress silver as the moon, and a dress glittering like the stars, along with a cloak made from patches of fur from every wild beast in the forest.

When the coats were delivered, the princess took three golden treasures—a ring, a tiny spinning wheel, and a reel—packed them inside a walnut shell, blackened her face with soot, wrapped herself in the fur cloak, and fled into the deep forest.

A neighboring king hunting with hounds discovered the creature in a hollow tree, named her Allerleirauh (All-Kinds-of-Fur), and put her to work in the palace kitchen sweeping ashes.

At three grand royal balls, she secretly washed the soot from her face, wore her sun, moon, and star dresses, and danced with the king, vanishing before midnight and leaving her golden treasures in the king's bread bowl.

On the third night, the king slipped a golden ring upon her finger. When she baked the bread in her fur cloak, the ring was found. The king seized her fur cloak, it slipped off, and her star-spangled dress and golden hair shone forth in royal beauty! The king embraced her, and their wedding was celebrated with great joy.
moral: True nobility cannot be obscured by rough fur; modesty and patient courage triumph over adversity.

title: Bearskin (Bärenhäuter)
full_text:
A discharged soldier left penniless after the wars met a mysterious stranger with a cloven foot. The stranger offered him limitless gold on one condition: for seven years, he must neither wash, shave, cut his hair, comb his beard, nor say his prayers, wearing only a heavy bearskin cloak. If he died within seven years, his soul was forfeited; if he survived, he was rich and free forever.

The soldier accepted. For several years he wandered, giving boundless alms to the poor so they would pray for him. Soon his face was blackened with grime, his hair matted like a mane, and people fled screaming from "Bearskin."

He stayed at an inn where he paid off the ruinous debts of an honest father. Grateful for his salvation, the father offered Bearskin one of his three daughters in marriage.

The two elder daughters turned away in disgust, mocking his hideous appearance. But the youngest daughter said gently: "He saved our father; I will keep my word to him!"

Bearskin broke his golden ring in two, gave her half, and kept the other, promising to return in three years.

When the seven years were fulfilled, the devil arrived, cursed in defeat, washed Bearskin clean, trimmed his beard, and dressed him in magnificent royal velvet.

Bearskin returned to the inn as a handsome nobleman. The two elder sisters flirted with him, while the youngest sat quietly in her mourning dress. Bearskin dropped his half of the ring into her wine cup; she recognized her faithful groom, and they were married with joyous celebration, teaching that true love beholds the soul, not the bearskin.
moral: Inner fidelity and quiet endurance of outward contempt win the true reward of love.

title: The Juniper Tree (Von dem Machandelboom)
full_text:
Beneath a fragrant juniper tree in the garden, a pious mother prayed for a child red as blood and white as snow. She bore a son, but died of joy, asking to be buried under the juniper tree.

The father remarried, and the second wife bore a daughter named Marlene. The stepmother loved Marlene, but despised the little boy, plotted his destruction, and killed him with a falling chest lid, cooking his flesh in a stew.

Little Marlene wept inconsolably. She gathered the little brother's bones in her silk kerchief and laid them beneath the fragrant juniper tree.

Suddenly, the tree rustled, mist rose from the branches, and out flew a magnificent golden bird singing with a voice of celestial beauty!

The bird flew through the town, singing its tragic tale to a goldsmith, a shoemaker, and twenty millers, receiving a golden chain, red shoes, and a heavy millstone in reward.

The bird flew back to the father's house, dropped the golden chain around the father's neck, dropped the red shoes for little Marlene, and dropped the heavy millstone upon the wicked stepmother, crushing her to dust!

In a flash of light, the brother stood whole and radiant once more, taking his father and sister by the hand, living in peace and eternal joy.
moral: Hidden murder cannot escape the justice of creation; truth sings through the branches.

title: The Six Swans
full_text:
A king lost in a great forest married a witch's daughter to find his way out. Fearing for his six sons and one daughter, he hid them in a secret castle in the woods, finding his way by a magical ball of yarn.

The wicked queen discovered the secret, sewed six shirts of enchanted white silk, and threw them over the six princes, transforming them into six wild swans that flew away over the forest.

The little sister walked into the wilderness to find her brothers. In a hut, the six swans arrived at sunset, shedding their feathers for fifteen minutes. They told her: "We can be saved only if you sew six shirts of star-flowers, and maintain absolute silence for six years without speaking or laughing!"

The maiden lived in a tall tree, sewing silently day and night.

A king found her, loved her quiet grace, and made her his queen. But his wicked mother stole the queen's newborn children, smeared her mouth with blood, and accused her of devouring them.

Even at the stake, the queen remained steadfastly silent, finishing the sixth shirt.

As the torch touched the wood, six swans flew down! She threw the shirts over them, and six handsome princes stood before the throne! Only the youngest had a swan's wing on his left arm, because the sleeve lacked a few stitches.

The queen spoke, declaring her innocence; the stolen children were restored, and the wicked mother-in-law was brought to justice.
moral: Patient, silent sacrifice endures all false accusations to redeem those we love.

title: Little Briar Rose (The Thorn Castle)
full_text:
Long ago, in a magnificent kingdom bordered by whispering pine forests, a king and queen rejoiced after many years of longing at the birth of a daughter of incomparable beauty. To celebrate the royal christening, the king held a grand feast, inviting the twelve wise fairy women of the realm. Alas, he possessed only twelve golden plates, so the thirteenth fairy was left uninvited. As the feast drew to a close, eleven fairies bestowed their miraculous blessings upon the golden cradle: radiant virtue, boundless wisdom, sweet melody, and grace. Suddenly, the bronze doors burst open, and the furious thirteenth fairy entered the hall. Pointing her iron staff at the infant, she hissed: 'In her fifteenth year, the king's daughter shall prick her finger on a spinning spindle, and fall down dead!'

Before the weeping parents could despair, the twelfth fairy stepped forward, whose gift was yet unspoken. 'The curse cannot be wholly revoked,' she spoke gently, 'yet it may be softened. The maiden shall not die, but fall into a deep, peaceful slumber that shall last for a hundred years.' To shield his darling child, the king commanded every spindle and spinning wheel in the entire realm to be burned to ashes. Yet on the very day of her fifteenth birthday, while wandering through the remote towers of the castle, the princess discovered a hidden spiral staircase leading to a tiny garret room. Inside sat an ancient woman spinning flax. Fascinated by the whirling wheel, the maiden reached out her hand to touch the spindle. The sharp point pricked her finger, and that very instant, she sank onto an embroidered couch in motionless slumber.

In that same moment, a magical stillness fell upon the entire palace. The king and queen fell asleep upon their thrones, the courtiers slept in the grand hall, the horses slept in the stables, the hounds in the courtyard, the doves upon the roof, and even the flies upon the stone walls. The crackling fire on the hearth ceased its flickering and fell asleep, while the roasting meat stopped sizzling. Around the silent castle grew a dense hedge of wild briar thorns, rising year after year until not even the weather-vanes atop the towers could be seen. Many brave princes attempted to force their way through the tangled thorns, but the briars seized them like iron claws. At last, when the hundred years had fully passed, a gentle prince arrived whose heart was pure. As he approached, the briar thorns burst into millions of fragrant crimson roses, parting willingly before his footsteps. Climbing the tower, he beheld the sleeping maiden, was overwhelmed by her radiant beauty, and bent down to bestow a tender kiss. Little Briar Rose opened her shining eyes, smiled with joy, and life, music, and laughter awakened across the entire kingdom once more.
moral: The appointed hour of providence dissolves every barrier of thorn and sleep.
